questions.q: What is the unit that fails over in a SQL Server Failover Cluster Instance (FCI)?
options: The entire SQL Server instance, including every database on it
A single named group of user databases
Only the transaction log files
Only the databases explicitly listed in an Availability Group
questions.explain: Unlike an AG, which fails over a named database group, an FCI fails over the whole instance as one all-or-nothing unit.

questions.q: What storage model does an FCI depend on that an Availability Group does not?
options: Shared storage — all cluster nodes point at the same disk, with only one node actively using it at a time
Each node has its own fully independent copy of the data, just like an AG
No storage at all is required for an FCI
FCI requires cloud-only storage and cannot use on-premises disks
questions.explain: FCI's defining feature is shared storage — nodes don't each hold a separate copy; they share one disk and only one node is active against it at a time.

questions.q: Why can't an FCI offer readable secondaries the way an AG can?
options: Because only one node is ever actively running against the shared storage at a time — there is no second independent copy to query
Because FCI does not support any client connections at all
Because readable secondaries are disabled by Microsoft licensing on FCI specifically
Because FCI always runs on more than two nodes simultaneously
questions.explain: Since every node shares the same underlying storage and only one is active, there's no separate replica available to serve read-only queries.

questions.q: Why does the shared storage itself become the most critical single point of failure in an FCI design?
options: Because if the underlying SAN or shared disk fails, no number of cluster nodes can save the instance, since they all depend on that same disk
Because shared storage has nothing to do with FCI's reliability
Because FCI automatically replicates the shared storage to a second, independent disk
Because cluster nodes each keep their own separate storage, making this a non-issue
questions.explain: All nodes depend on the same shared disk, so protecting that storage (or pairing FCI with a separate DR mechanism) matters more than adding cluster nodes.

questions.q: Which scenario, per this lesson, would lead a DBA to choose an FCI over Availability Groups?
options: Shared storage (a SAN) already exists in the environment, and protecting the whole instance — including system databases — in one failover event is simpler than managing many AGs
The team specifically wants multiple readable secondary copies for reporting
The databases need to fail over independently of each other on different schedules
The environment has no shared storage available anywhere
questions.explain: FCI fits when shared storage already exists and whole-instance (including system database) protection is preferred over per-database AG management.
